title: Check My Modelling
author: Cognitive Coaching
summary: A short entry in the Coaching Cuts series, built around a video of coach Adam working with coachee Katie. The technique has a clean name: check my modelling. The coach runs the model themselves, and the coachee watches from the student's seat, checking that the model actually delivers what a student needs to take away. The frame flips the usual coaching gaze. Instead of the coachee watching for technique, they are watching for landing. The prerequisites matter and the piece is explicit about them. Before the model runs, coach and coachee agree on what the students must take away, and they codify it as a simple success criterion. Adam models a modelling task (he is drawing a model while modelling drawing a model, which the author cheerfully flags), narrates his thinking, and afterwards asks Katie, 'How close was I to the success criteria for the kids?' That question is the hinge. It forces the coachee to evaluate against a shared external standard rather than a generic impression of clarity. The why is the piece's strongest turn for primary-classroom use. Models only work if they land. Teachers routinely assume their modelling was clear because it was clear to them, and miss that students lost the key moves, misread the reasoning, or got absorbed in surface detail. Running the check against an agreed criterion surfaces those blind spots in a way post-hoc observation rarely does. The cautions are equally useful: do not run this technique when the coachee is already cognitively overloaded, and do not run it without a shared definition of good, or the analysis drifts into opinion.
points: The central argument of this piece is grounded in the author's engagement with how real people think and act, not in idealized or abstract reasoning.
The takeaway is actionable,it can be implemented at the classroom or school level without waiting for policy change or external resources.
The piece challenges a common default assumption in education practice and offers a concrete alternative framed by evidence or lived experience.
The stakes are clear: what happens if leaders or teachers adopt this approach, and what is the cost of continuing the current default.
quotes: In this post, we see coach Adam do something similar with coachee, Katie, with a model he does himself. He wants Katie to experience the model as if she’s a student in the class and check he does and narrates all the steps the children need to know.
Check my modelling is where the coach puts the coachee in the position of the students and gets them to check that the model does what it needs to do.

We want our coachees to pay close attention to the models we show them. Getting them to analyse our modelling through the eyes of a student is a great idea for securing this attention and ensures they are thinking ‘Will this hit home for my students?

What you don’t see in this clip is that Katie and Adam spend a chunk of time beforehand deciding on what children must take away from this modelling. Adam then gets Katie to watch his model and analyse it through that lens to start with.

This allows her to see the power of his model for clearly communicating the process and reasoning behind it through narrating his thinking. We join them part way through Adam modelling. Listen for how he asks Katie afterwards to consider “How close was I to the success criteria for the kids?

Because models only work if they land for students. Teachers often assume their modelling is clear, but students can easily miss the key moves, misunderstand the reasoning, or get lost in surface detail.

By asking a coachee to experience the model “as a student,” you might surface these blind spots. Use it when the coachee already understands what they’re trying to model and what students must take from it. You have agreed a clear, simple success criterion for the modelling.

Avoid or delay it when it risks cognitive overload: if the coachee is juggling too many new ideas at once, focusing on modelling quality won’t be productive. You haven’t aligned on what “good” looks like; without a shared success criterion, the analysis becomes vague.” Archived from Cognitive Coaching on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
